resend.title: How to get Resend credentials
resend.step1: Sign in to your Resend account at resend.com.
resend.step2: Navigate to API Keys and click "Create API Key" (select Sending or Full Access).
resend.step3: In Domains, verify your sending domain (or use onboarding@resend.dev for testing).
resend.step4: Paste your API key (re_...) and sender email on the left.

uploadthing.title: How to get UploadThing credentials
uploadthing.step1: Log in to your UploadThing dashboard at uploadthing.com.
uploadthing.step2: Select your application or click "Create App".
uploadthing.step3: Go to API Keys in the sidebar to view your UPLOADTHING_TOKEN.
uploadthing.step4: Copy and paste the secret token (starts with eyJ...) into the field on the left.

ai.title: How to get AI API keys
ai.step1: Choose your preferred LLM provider(s) from Google Gemini, DeepSeek, OpenAI, or Anthropic.
ai.step2: Google Gemini (Recommended): Get a free/pay-as-you-go key from Google AI Studio for fast ATS resume scoring & interview prep.
ai.step3: DeepSeek: Generate an API key (sk-...) in the DeepSeek Open Platform console.
ai.step4: OpenAI: Generate a secret API key (sk-proj-...) in the OpenAI Platform dashboard.
ai.step5: Anthropic: Create an API key (sk-ant-...) in the Anthropic Console for Claude models.

spotify.title: How to configure Spotify OAuth
spotify.step1: Sign in to the Spotify Developer Dashboard.
spotify.step2: Click "Create App", enter an app name, and select Web API.
spotify.step3: In App Settings, add the exact Redirect URI shown below.
spotify.step4: Copy your Client ID and Client Secret, then paste them to connect.

googleCalendar.title: How to configure Google Calendar OAuth
googleCalendar.step1: Open Google Cloud Console > APIs & Services > Credentials.
googleCalendar.step2: Create an OAuth 2.0 Client ID (Application type: Web application).
googleCalendar.step3: Add the exact Authorized Redirect URI shown below.
googleCalendar.step4: Enable the Google Calendar API in APIs & Services > Library.
googleCalendar.step5: Copy your Client ID and Client Secret into the form.

qaCollaboration.metaDescription: How I work with QA teams — self-review, test planning, bug validation, and release readiness built into every release.

hero.title: Quality-first engineering, built into
hero.description: I review, test, and validate my own code before QA ever sees it — then work side by side with QA on test planning, execution, and bug validation, so releases ship with fewer surprises and less back-and-forth.
hero.scrollHint: Scroll to how I work with QA

benefits.title: What this means for your project

0.title: Fewer bugs reach production
0.description: I review and test my own code before QA does, catching issues early instead of after a release.

1.title: QA gets a real partner
1.description: I support test planning, execution, and bug validation directly with QA — not just tickets thrown over a wall.

2.title: Tests that actually cover the code
2.description: Unit and integration tests around critical paths, written as part of the work, not bolted on after.

3.title: Fewer surprises at release
3.description: Manual QA and regression testing catch what automated tests can't — before release, not during it.

4.title: Clarity on what's tested and what's risky
4.description: You know what's covered, what isn't, and what still needs attention before a release ships.

5.title: Quality habits that scale to a team
5.description: Practices I've carried into leading engineering teams of up to 6, not just my own code.

0.title: Self-review before handoff
0.description: Before anything reaches QA, I review my own code and run it through unit and integration tests, so the obvious issues never leave my branch.

1.title: Test planning support
1.description: I help define what needs testing — critical flows, edge cases, risk areas — so QA's time goes to the right places first.

2.title: Clear handoff
2.description: Bugs and features go to QA with context: what changed, what to check, how to reproduce edge cases.

3.title: Working QA's tickets, not just mine
3.description: I pick up bug reports directly, reproduce issues, and fix them with QA in the loop — not weeks later in a separate cycle.

4.title: Bug validation together
4.description: Once a fix is in, I validate it with QA before it's marked resolved — not just "should be fixed."

5.title: Regression & release readiness
5.description: Before a release, I help review what's changed, what's covered, and what's still a risk — so "ready to ship" actually means something.

roles.title: Where I fit in the QA process
roles.description: Full-Stack Developer and Software Architect, working directly alongside the rest of the QA ecosystem — not around it.

0.question: Does reviewing your own code replace QA?
0.answer: No — it complements it. Catching the obvious issues early means QA's time goes to deeper testing and edge cases, not restating what a careful pass would've caught.

1.question: Do you work with an existing QA team, or instead of one?
1.answer: With. I plug into test planning, bug validation, and release readiness alongside QA — I'm not a substitute for a QA process.

2.question: Is this just manual review, or do you write automated tests too?
2.answer: Both. Unit and integration tests around critical paths, plus a manual pass before anything reaches QA.

3.question: What if the team doesn't have a clear QA process yet?
3.answer: I can help make testing scope, priorities, and reproduction steps clearer as part of how I work — not by taking over QA's role, but by making the handoff easier.

4.question: Doesn't extra review slow releases down?
4.answer: The opposite, in practice — fewer bugs reaching QA or production means less back-and-forth, which is usually what actually slows a release down.

cta.title: Want QA and dev to actually work together?
cta.description: Let's talk about your project, your release process, and where I can help.

howIUseAi.metaDescription: How I integrate AI into daily software engineering — from discovery and planning to code review, QA, documentation, and delivery.

hero.title: AI-native software engineering, built into
hero.description: I design, build, test, and deliver software with AI woven into my day-to-day — from research and planning to code review and delivery updates — while ownership, quality, and visibility stay in my hands.

benefits.title: What this means for your project

0.title: Faster delivery, same standards
0.description: AI speeds up research, boilerplate, and testing — the engineering judgment behind every decision stays mine.

1.title: More than just code
1.description: Planning, QA, documentation, and delivery visibility are part of how I work — not afterthoughts.

2.title: Clear visibility into progress
2.description: Regular, honest updates on progress, blockers, and what's next — no surprises at delivery.

3.title: AI used responsibly
3.description: Every AI-assisted output goes through my own review before it ships. I stay accountable for the outcome.

4.title: Realistic estimates
4.description: AI-assisted planning helps me scope work accurately before I commit to a timeline.

5.title: Quality that holds up
5.description: AI-assisted testing and review catch issues earlier, without replacing careful engineering judgment.

steps.title: How I integrate AI into my day-to-day
steps.description: Six stages, one workflow — AI supports each of them, judgment drives all of them. Click a stage to see it in practice.

0.title: Discovery & research
0.description: Before writing code, I use AI to move faster through unfamiliar domains, APIs, edge cases, and prior art — then verify anything I'll actually rely on against the real documentation.
0.detail: I'll ask Claude or ChatGPT for a fast first pass on a new API, library, or approach — but I don't take it at face value. Anything I'm going to build on gets checked against the real documentation before I write a line of code.

1.title: Planning & estimation
1.description: AI helps me break work into tickets, flag risks early, and sanity-check estimates against similar past work — I still make the final call.
1.detail: I'll paste in a feature description and ask for a task breakdown, then adjust it against what I actually know about the codebase. It's a first draft I edit, not a plan I follow blindly.

2.title: Development
2.description: I pair with tools like GitHub Copilot and Claude for boilerplate, refactors, and exploring approaches. Every architectural decision is mine.
2.detail: GitHub Copilot handles inline completions while I'm typing. For bigger chunks I describe what I need and review the output line by line before it goes in. I don't ship code I don't understand.

3.title: Code review & QA
3.description: AI is wired into my pipeline and PR checks — flagging vulnerabilities, code smells, and likely bugs — so issues surface before manual QA and my own review even start.
3.detail: I've got AI checks running in my CI pipeline and on every pull request. None of that replaces my own review — I triage every flag myself, since not everything it raises is worth acting on.
3.tools: Tools: Claude, GitHub Copilot, CI/CD checks

4.title: Documentation
4.description: AI turns code and decisions into docs, PR descriptions, and onboarding notes that are far more likely to stay current.
4.detail: PR descriptions, changelogs, and README updates start as an AI-generated first pass based on my diff and commit messages. I edit for accuracy, but documentation actually happens instead of being skipped.

5.title: Delivery & communication
5.description: Status updates, changelogs, and client-facing summaries start as AI-assisted drafts — I edit and own everything before it goes out.
5.detail: When it's time to report progress, I'll turn completed tickets into a clear, non-technical summary with AI, then edit the tone and add context only I have.

toolkit.title: Tools I bring into the workflow
toolkit.description: The mix changes per project. Tap a tool to see what it's actually for.
toolkit.footnote: Tool choice adapts to each project's stack and constraints.

0.name: GitHub Copilot
0.description: Inline completions while I'm actively coding, plus automated PR checks that flag vulnerabilities, code smells, and improvement suggestions before a human looks at the diff.

1.name: Claude
1.description: Planning, refactors, documentation, drafting client-facing updates, and flagging the edge cases in QA most likely to turn into real bugs.

2.name: ChatGPT
2.description: Quick research and comparing approaches when I'm outside my usual stack.

3.name: Cursor
3.description: AI-native editor for larger, multi-file changes, exploring unfamiliar codebases, and quickly prototyping a feasibility demo before I commit to an approach.

4.name: Perplexity
4.description: Fast, sourced answers when I need to verify something technical quickly.

5.name: v0
5.description: Scaffolding quick UI demos to validate an idea before I rebuild it properly by hand.

6.name: Notion AI
6.description: Turning meeting notes and scattered thoughts into structured project docs.

0.question: Does using AI mean less code review?
0.answer: No — every AI-assisted change goes through the same review process as anything else I write. AI speeds up the first draft, not the standard.

1.question: What if a client doesn't want AI involved?
1.answer: That's fine — I scope around it. AI is how I work faster, not a requirement for the project.

2.question: Do you let AI make architecture decisions?
2.answer: No. I use it to explore options and stress-test ideas, but architecture and technical direction stay mine.

3.question: How do you keep AI-assisted code reliable?
3.answer: The same way I keep any code reliable: testing, review, and holding it to the same bar regardless of how it was written.

4.question: Which AI tools do you actually use day to day?
4.answer: Mostly GitHub Copilot and Claude for coding, and ChatGPT or Perplexity for research — the mix shifts by project.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.metaDescription: How we handle your data, including anonymous audience measurement and Spotify credentials.
privacy.subtitle: How we handle your data
privacy.intro: This portfolio platform stores only the data needed to provide its features. This page explains anonymous audience measurement on public pages and what we collect if you connect Spotify.

spotify.title: Spotify integration
spotify.intro: If you connect Spotify in the admin panel, we store credentials for your own Spotify developer app so the Now Playing widget can show playback on your public portfolio.
spotify.storedClientSecret: Your Spotify app Client Secret, encrypted at rest
spotify.storedRefreshToken: Your Spotify refresh token, encrypted at rest
spotify.storedScope: The OAuth scopes granted during authorization
spotify.purpose: We use this data only to request Spotify playback information on your behalf for visitors to your portfolio. We do not sell or share it with third parties.
spotify.disconnect: You can disconnect Spotify at any time from Admin → Spotify. Disconnecting deletes your Spotify tokens and app credentials from our database immediately.
spotify.retention: If you disconnect or ask us to stop processing your Spotify data, we delete it without undue delay and within five days at most, in line with Spotify's developer terms.

analytics.title: Audience measurement
analytics.intro: Public pages send a small first-party beacon so the owner can see approximate traffic. This is not advertising or cross-site tracking, and it does not set cookies.
analytics.storedPageviews: Daily totals of pageviews and session visits, grouped by page path, country, and referrer hostname
analytics.notStoredId: Cookies, fingerprints, or unique visitor identifiers
analytics.notStoredCity: City-level location (country only, from the hosting platform)
analytics.purpose: We use these aggregates only to show stats on the public /stats page and in the portfolio admin. Data is not sold or shared with analytics vendors.
analytics.optOut: If your browser sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control, we skip the measurement entirely.
analytics.retention: Aggregates older than 13 months are deleted.
